title: Head‑to‑head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes — Validator‑Acceptance Parity under Shared‑Candidate Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) that measured validator‑acceptance parity for intent→configuration NetOps changes under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Two downstream architectures were compared given the same LLM candidate per task: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run used gpt‑5‑mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for end‑to‑end checks. Execution completed 240 episodes (120 paired tasks) with a single shared generation per pair (model_calls_used = 120). Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (both arms accepted all 120 candidates). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because generation was intentionally shared, these outcomes measure validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates and do not adjudicate independent generator or repair robustness. We provide artifact‑grounded evidence, an explicit evidence‑to‑claim mapping, a compact nearest‑work comparison, and preregistered protocol modifications required to obtain a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison in follow‑ups.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation and safe sequencing of multi‑vendor NetOps changes is operationally critical: production networks require correctness guarantees (reachability, isolation, absence of transient safety violations) while supporting diverse vendor CLIs and operator intents. Two architectural families are common: (1) translation‑first pipelines that constrain generation via a vendor‑aware DSL and apply formal verification/solver-based synthesis to ensure device-level guarantees; and (2) agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines that centralize generation in an LLM and rely on deterministic validators and bounded repair or rollback to achieve correctness while preserving generator flexibility.

This study preregistered (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) a paired design to compare end‑to‑end operational correctness between those architectures for intent tasks spanning heterogeneous vendor grammars and Mininet‑derived topologies. Final research question (preregistered): For intent‑driven network changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and realistic emulator topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness (measured by deterministic validation of reachability and policy isolation) — (A) translation‑first or (B) agentic generate→validate→repair?

Contributions. (1) A preregistered, fully archived paired experiment that implemented shared_initial_candidate semantics and precise deterministic scoring; (2) an explicit evidence‑to‑claim table that maps preregistered hypotheses to measured estimands and archived artifacts; (3) a compact nearest‑work comparison situating this validator‑parity measurement among recent translation→verify and LLM‑agent studies; (4) concrete, artifact‑grounded protocol modifications enabling a discriminating follow‑up (remove shared_candidate, increase model calls, enable repair instrumentation). We emphasize up front that, by design, the present run isolates validator acceptance for identical candidates and therefore does not test independent generator variance or repair coverage.
sections.related_work:
Two literatures bound our contribution. Formal translation→verification work emphasizes constrained generation with deterministic guarantees and solver‑based synthesis; classical network verification, synthesis, and Weighted NetKAT families are representative [10,11,12]. LLM and agentic NetOps work explores flexible generation, multi‑tool orchestration, and iterative repair but stresses the need for deterministic validators to bound hallucination and unsafe proposals [3,4,5]. Recent NetOps and AIOps benchmarks and tutorials document both evaluation axes and safety concerns [2,6].

Nearest‑work compact matrix (selected entries). We compare four experimental axes: independent generation sampling (IG), repair loop instrumentation (RL), validator‑acceptance focus (VA), and emulator/hardware realism (EH).
• INTA (ICNP 2025) [3]: IG = yes; RL = limited; VA = partial; EH = emulator.
• Mahmood & Song (IFIP Networking 2026) [4]: IG = yes; RL = yes; VA = emphasized; EH = Kubernetes policy domain.
• Weighted NetKAT / formal verification family [5,10–12]: IG = n/a; RL = solver‑based; VA = core; EH = verification models.
• Present run (CAND‑2026‑001): IG = no (shared_initial_candidate); RL = instrumented but no repairs observed; VA = primary; EH = Mininet‑derived emulation.

This run differs by explicitly preregistering shared candidate semantics and producing per‑task deterministic validator traces archived for audit; the measurement is therefore a validator‑acceptance parity test rather than an independent architectural showdown.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed the primary estimand: paired difference in binary end‑to‑end correctness (A − B) across N = 120 paired tasks. Design parameters included planned_episode_count = 240, maximum_model_calls = 240, declared generator = gpt‑5‑mini, validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0), execution adapter = hosted_netops_gvr_v1, and allowed repair_iterations = 1. The preregistration specifically implemented shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single LLM generation per paired task is supplied identically to both downstream arms; this choice removes generator variance from the confirmatory estimand and focuses the test on validator acceptance parity.

Task corpus and task generator. Confirmatory tasks (N = 120 pairs) were produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each task manifest entry includes: intent natural language, initial and expected final states, required safe sequences (make‑before‑break, shutdown→modify→restore patterns), canonical reference answers, and difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count). Representative entries (task‑000001, task‑000002, task‑000003, ...) and the full task manifest are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl.

Orchestration, shared_candidate semantics, and execution accounting. Orchestration executed a single LLM generation per pair (shared_initial_candidate) and provided the identical text candidate to both the translation‑first and agentic arms. The execution manifest records planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Provider audit records hosted_model_call_event_count = 120 and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false, demonstrating per‑call isolation consistent with the preregistered contamination controls.

Validator and scoring mechanics. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applies full_intent_constraint_validation rules: syntactic normalization, required command inclusion, ordering/dependency checks, and final state consistency; validation_after.valid is the binary end‑to‑end correctness indicator. Per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task‑000XXX‑*.json) record normalized_response, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before/after snapshots, and repair_applied flags. A configuration passes only if validation_after.valid == true. Repair prompts and any repair_applied decisions are recorded in the per‑episode traces.

Statistical analysis executor. Analysis followed the preregistered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor: compute contingency counts (n11,n10,n01,n00), paired difference (A − B), bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729), and an exact McNemar two‑sided test for paired binary outcomes. Secondary estimands (repair coverage, mean repair iterations) and multiplicity adjustments (Benjamini–Hochberg for subgroup tests) were preregistered. All analysis parameters and seeds are archived (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcomes. The run completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 240 with model_calls_used = 120 (single shared generation per pair). Deterministic scoring across the 120 complete pairs produced contingency counts: n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Marginal success rates: baseline = 120/120 = 1.0 and guarded = 120/120 = 1.0. The paired difference (A − B) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Analysis artifacts include analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv.

Repair behavior and secondary outcomes. Aggregated repair_applied count = 0 across all 240 episodes (execution/scoring/*.json show repair_applied = false per episode). Consequently preregistered secondary estimands concerning repair coverage (H2) are unobserved in this execution; the artifacts show the repair instrumentation was active but not triggered by any shared candidate. Per‑task traces (e.g., execution/scoring/task‑000001‑baseline.json) show validation_before.valid == validation_after.valid == true and repair_applied == false for representative tasks.

Contamination, missingness, and audit checks. Contamination checks raised no flags: analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty and analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120 with zero missing or failed episodes. Provider audit shows cache_miss_count = 120 and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false, supporting execution isolation as preregistered. Deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms episode accounting and marginal contingency consistency.

Representative example. Pair‑000001: the shared LLM candidate matched the canonical reference modulo normalization and ordering; validator parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, validation_after.valid = true, repair_applied = false. Similar representative artifacts for multiple pairs are archived and cited in the execution manifest.

Interpretation of numeric results. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the observed degenerate concordance (all pairs concordant) indicates validator‑acceptance parity for the identical candidates: both downstream validator toolchains accepted every provided candidate. The statistical descriptors (point estimate zero difference, degenerate bootstrap CI, McNemar p = 1.0) accurately describe this observed dataset but must be read in the context of the narrower estimand the design implemented.
sections.discussion:
What was measured and what remains untested. The preregistered shared_initial_candidate design intentionally removed generator variance; the primary estimand tested here is therefore validator‑acceptance parity for identical LLM candidates rather than independent generator correctness or repair robustness. The evidence confirms parity: every shared candidate was accepted by both arms. However, independent sampling effects, model variance across multiple generations, and repair coverage under initial failures were not exercised and remain untested by this run.

Evidence‑to‑claim mapping (compact table narrative). H1 (Paired difference A − B): measured estimand = validator‑acceptance parity under shared_initial_candidate semantics; supporting artifacts: execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0), analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (bootstrap parameters). Verdict: tested, measured estimand narrower than original high‑level hypothesis. H2 (Agentic pipeline higher repair coverage): observed? no — repair_applied = 0 for all episodes; supporting artifacts: execution/scoring/*.json (repair_applied = false). Verdict: unobserved in this execution.

Operational implications and recommended follow‑ups. The present protocol is appropriate as a validator regression and equivalence test: when operators or developers wish to assert that different orchestration stacks will accept the same proposed changes, the shared_candidate design and deterministic validator traces provide reproducible evidence. To discriminate the architectures on independent generator or repair performance, the preregistered follow‑ups should: (i) remove shared_initial_candidate so each arm receives an independent generation per pair (model_calls_used would increase from 120 to 240 for initial candidates alone); (ii) sample multiple candidate generations per arm to estimate generator variance; (iii) enable and instrument repair iterations so repair_applied > 0 can be observed and quantified; (iv) consider higher‑fidelity device validation to reduce emulator‑to‑hardware contamination risk. Each modification produces machine‑verifiable changes in the execution manifest (increased hosted_model_call_event_count, nonzero repair flags) and therefore supports clear auditability.

Threats to validity (expanded). Internal validity: the shared candidate removes generator variance and narrows the estimand; results are internally consistent but intentionally limited. Construct validity: deterministic validator acceptance operationalizes correctness per ruleset but omits operator‑facing dimensions (explainability, maintainability). External validity: synthetic task corpus and Mininet‑derived emulation limit generalization to production hardware; single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) further restrict multi‑model/validator conclusions. Conclusion validity: degenerate concordance produces point mass CIs and noninformative p‑values for architecture superiority under independent operation.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, fully archived paired experiment comparing translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair NetOps pipelines under shared_initial_candidate semantics. For 120 paired tasks the deterministic validator accepted the identical LLM candidates in both arms for all pairs (n11 = 120, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0), yielding paired difference 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). No repairs were applied (repair_applied = false for all 240 episodes); preregistered hypotheses about repair coverage are therefore unobserved. The run demonstrates how preregistered shared‑candidate experiments precisely measure validator‑acceptance parity but, by design, do not adjudicate independent generator or repair robustness. We provide artifact‑grounded evidence, an explicit evidence‑to‑claim mapping, and concrete preregistered protocol modifications that would enable a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison in follow‑ups.

limitations: Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were used; this intentionally removes generator variance and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.

The task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
A single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

The binary deterministic validator acceptance metric does not capture operator‑facing properties such as explanation quality, maintainability, or human trust, which matter in production but were outside the metric used here.
